Every model has a population: how many people there are, their ages and sex, and anything else about them that the model needs, such as where they live. This page covers the size of the population, its ages (including the population of a named country), other properties of people and how a model uses them, and, for a model run as agents, the [`People`](../api/people.qmd) object that holds what each agent is and has, and the arrays it keeps them in. Births, deaths, and migration are in [Demographics](populations_demographics.qmd), and who meets whom is in [Contact networks](populations_networks.qmd).

The examples use the measles model from the tutorials:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
```

## How many people

`total_pop=` is the number of people in the population. A model run as compartments needs nothing else:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
```

As agents, `n_agents=` is the number of agents. Given both, each agent stands for `total_pop/n_agents` people, here 10, and results are given in people, not agents:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()
```

The two runs differ a little, since as agents the epidemic is a stochastic process that takes whole daily steps (see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd)). Without either `total_pop=` or `n_agents=`, a model has 10,000 people. Fewer agents than people make a model faster, but add noise from chance, more so for rare events; see [Branching and rescaling](running_branching.qmd).

## Ages and sex

As agents, each person has an age and a sex. Unless told otherwise, Starsim gives agents the ages of the world's population in 2024, and an even chance of being female; `ss.People(n_agents, p_female=0.49)` gives another share of women (`p_female=0` makes a population of men only, e.g. for a model of men who have sex with men). A compartmental model split into age groups without a share for each takes the shares from the same ages, and `describe()` marks them as guessed.

The population of a country is `ss.population()`: its size, its ages, and its share of women, from the UN World Population Prospects (or, for a US state, the US Census), which come with Starsim. The sim takes its size from it, so a compartmental model can use a named population as well as agents can:

```{python}
kenya = ss.population('Kenya', year=2024)
print('Population of Kenya in 2024:', round(kenya.named.total))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, people=ss.population('Kenya', year=2024, n_agents=5000), stop=ss.days(50))
sim.init()
sim.people.plot_ages();
```

In a compartmental model, ages matter only once the model is split into age groups, with `measles.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65])`, which then takes the share of people in each group from the named population. See [Stratification](building_stratification.qmd) and, for contacts between age groups, [Population data](populations_data.qmd). The tutorial [T4 – Age groups and contacts](../tutorials/t4_ages.qmd) builds an age-structured measles model step by step.

Ages can also come from data of your own, with `ss.People(n_agents, age_data=...)`: a table with a column `age` (the lower edge of each age group) and a column `value` (the number or share of people in it), or a CSV file with those columns:

```{python}
ppl = ss.People(5000, age_data='test_data/nigeria_age.csv')
sim = ss.Sim(measles, people=ppl, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.init()
sim.people.plot_ages();
```

A sim copies the people it is given when it is built, so look at `sim.people` afterwards, not at `ppl`.

## Properties of people

A model refers to a property of people with `ss.person`: `ss.person.age`, `ss.person.female`, or a property of your own. `ss.person.age < 5` is a condition, which picks out people, for example to say who an intervention reaches:

```python
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.8, where=ss.person.age < 5, at=ss.days(10)) # Vaccinates children under 5
```

A property of your own is given to `ss.People` as a state, with a value for each agent; it can be drawn from a distribution. A property can be in a rate as well as in a condition. Here 30% of people live in towns, where crowding doubles the rate at which a susceptible person is infected, and 92% of people are immune (as from routine vaccination), so that measles can still spread. Two campaigns give the same number of doses, to 27% of people: one to anyone, and one to 90% of the people in towns:

```{python}
urban = ss.BoolState('urban', default=ss.bernoulli(p=0.3))
ppl = ss.People(10_000, extra_states=urban)

infection = S >> I @ 1.9*(1 + ss.person.urban)*I # Twice the rate in towns
measles_towns = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.92), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

anyone = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.27, at=ss.days(1), name='campaign')
towns = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.9, where=ss.person.urban, at=ss.days(1), name='campaign')
base = ss.Sim(measles_towns, people=ppl, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No campaign': base,
    'Campaign, anyone': base.new(interventions=anyone),
    'Campaign, towns': base.new(interventions=towns),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')
for sim in msim.sims:
    print(sim.label, '- infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))
```

With no campaign, measles infects about 470 of the 800 people who are not immune. A campaign for anyone cuts that by more than half, and the same doses given in towns cut it further, since each of them goes to someone at twice the risk, and it is the people at most risk who keep the outbreak going. A property such as `urban` matters in a model as much as it changes who is infected and who is reached.

`ss.person` is read when the sim is built, so the property can be given after the model is written.

In a compartmental model, people have no properties of their own, only the groups the model is split into. The same property is a stratification, and the same model and conditions then work on groups, with the people in towns as 30% of the population:

```{python}
measles_groups = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.92), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
measles_groups.stratify(urban={False: 0.7, True: 0.3}) # 70% rural, 30% in towns

for label, campaign in {'No campaign': None, 'Campaign, anyone': anyone, 'Campaign, towns': towns}.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(measles_groups, interventions=campaign, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    print(label, '- infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))
sim.results.measles.I.by('urban').plot()
```

The compartmental model gives much the same numbers as the agents with no campaign, and with a campaign for anyone; with the campaign in towns, it gives about half as many infections as the agents did. Near the threshold for an outbreak (here, the campaign in towns brings the effective reproduction number close to 1), the course of an outbreak depends on chance, which agents have and an ODE does not, so a single run of agents is not the whole answer: see [Scenarios](running_scenarios.qmd).

## States and arrays

As agents, what each person is and has is kept in arrays with one value per agent. A state such as `alive`, `female`, or a disease's `I` is an `ss.BoolState`, an array of true or false values; a number, such as `age`, is an `ss.FloatArr` (or `ss.IntArr` for whole numbers). These arrays work like NumPy arrays, with sums, means, comparisons, and arithmetic, but are made for three things nearly every agent-based model needs:

1. **Growth**: as people are born or arrive, the arrays grow, in chunks rather than one agent at a time, so that adding agents is cheap.
2. **Indexing**: agents who die or leave stay in the arrays, so that what happened to them can still be looked up, but are left out of counts, sums, and means.
3. **Random values**: a state's default can be a distribution, as with `urban` above, so each new agent draws its own value, with [common random numbers](mechanics_random.qmd) so that two runs give each agent the same draw.

Every agent has a UID, its identifier, which never changes and is its position in the full ("raw") arrays. The UIDs of the agents still taking part (alive and not removed) are `people.auids`, the active UIDs. Most of the time you won't need these, but here is how they work, in a population with births and deaths (at default rates) over 20 years:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=1000, start='2000', stop='2020', dt=ss.years(1), demographics=True, verbose=0)
sim.init()
ppl = sim.people
print('Agents at the start:', len(ppl))
print('Mean age at the start:', ppl.age.mean())

sim.run()
print('Births:', sim.results.population.births.sum())
print('Deaths:', sim.results.died.sum())
print('Agents at the end:', len(ppl))
print('UIDs used:', ppl.uid.raw.max() + 1)
print('Length of the raw arrays:', len(ppl.age.raw))
print('Mean age of the living:', ppl.age.mean())
```

The number of agents is the number of living agents. The UIDs used include the agents who have died, and the raw arrays are a little longer still, with room for the next births. `ppl.age.values` gives the values for the active agents, and `ppl.age.raw` for every slot, including empty ones (which hold NaN). A condition on an array gives the UIDs of the agents who meet it, and those UIDs index any other array:

```{python}
under5 = (ppl.age < 5).uids
print('Children under 5:', len(under5))
print('Share of them who are female:', ppl.female[under5].mean())
print('UIDs of the first few who died:', ppl.dead.uids[:5])
```

For how to pick out agents in code, see [Array indexing](mechanics_indexing.qmd).

## People as agents

As agents, `sim.people` holds every agent: its properties, and the states of every module in the sim. Each person has these:

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| `alive` | Whether the agent is alive |
| `female` | Whether the agent is female |
| `age` | The agent's age, in years |
| `ti_dead` | The step on which the agent died, if it has (NaN otherwise) |
| `ti_removed` | The step on which the agent left for another reason, such as emigration |
| `cause_of_death` | The cause of each death (its position in `people.causes`, the names of the causes; -1 for none) |
| `scale` | The number of people the agent stands for, relative to the others (1 unless set) |

Each module adds its own states, under its name. A declared disease adds a state for each of its states (`sim.people.measles.S`, `.I`, `.R`), the time each agent entered a state (`ti_I`) and is due to leave it, and each person's relative susceptibility and transmissibility (`rel_sus` and `rel_trans`). To save memory, the time of entering a state is kept only when something reads it: the disease itself (e.g. for a state with a dwell time), or the code of a module in the sim that names it. Reading one that wasn't kept, e.g. in an analysis after the run, raises an error that says so; `ss.State(keep_time=True)` keeps it for one state (e.g. for code that reads the time since onset), and `ss.Sim(..., keep_times=True)` keeps them all, and the history of every transition (e.g. `sir.infection.n_times`), for that sim (`ss.options.keep_times = True` does so for every sim).

A time of entering reads as the step the move happened in, so `ti_E.isclose(sim.ti)` is "entered this step". The difference of two of them is not always a duration, though: an infection by contact happens at the end of its step, and a scheduled move (such as becoming infectious after a latent period) at the start of its step, so `ti_I - ti_E` reads one step longer than the latent period was. For the time people spent in a state, use the state's `stays`: `np.mean(sim.diseases.measles.E.stays)` is the mean latent period, a duration in the sim's unit, over everyone who has entered E and left it. Those still in the state are left out (`E.time_in` gives how long they have been there so far). With each state whose time of entering is kept, the time each person last left it is kept too, so `stays` works for any such state, e.g. one with a dwell time (`I.stays` in an SIR); for another, keep its time as above.

A module adds its states to the people when the sim is initialized, so they don't need to be given to `ss.People`. A property that belongs to one module (such as a disease's immunity) is best defined in that module, with `define_states()` (see [Custom modules](building_modules.qmd)); a property that several modules use (such as `urban`, or a social determinant of health) is best given to `ss.People` with `extra_states=`, as above.

## States with several columns

Sometimes each person needs several values of the same kind, such as their immunity to each of several strains. A state can have `columns=`, which gives it one row per agent and one column per value. Like any state, it grows as agents are born. Here a [module written as code](building_modules.qmd) keeps each person's susceptibility to two strains, and the susceptibility to the second one falls by 10% each year:

```{python}
class Immunity(ss.Module):
    """ Susceptibility to two strains, with susceptibility to the second falling over time """
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('sus', columns=['wild', 'mutant'], default=1.0),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        self.sus.mutant *= 0.9**(self.t.dt/ss.years(1)) # The second column, for every agent: 10% less each year
        return

sim = ss.Sim(Immunity(), n_agents=1000, demographics=True, start='2000', stop='2005', dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sus = sim.people.immunity.sus
print('Number of agents:', len(sim.people))
print('Shape of the values:', sus.values.shape)
```

A column can be read by name as an attribute (`sus.mutant`), as a key (`sus['mutant']`), or with `sus.col('mutant')`; each gives an ordinary array with one value per agent, and writing to it (`sus.mutant = 0`) changes the state. To index, the first index picks agents and the second picks columns, by name or by position:

```{python}
uids = ss.uids([0, 1, 2])
print('Both columns, for 3 agents:')
print(sus[uids])
print('The mutant column, for 3 agents:', sus[uids, 'mutant'])
print('Mean susceptibility to the mutant:', sus.mutant.mean())

sus[uids, 'wild'] = 0 # These agents are now immune to the wild type
print('Immune to the wild type:', (sus.col('wild') < 0.5).uids)
```

Since a state with several columns has several values per agent, it can't be turned into UIDs directly; use one column, as above. Some other things to note:

- `columns=3` gives three unnamed columns, read by position only, and a tuple such as `columns=(2, 3)` gives more dimensions.
- Column names must be unique, and can't be the name of something an array already has (such as `raw` or `mean`).
- `sus[:, [0, 1]]` gives columns 0 and 1 for every active agent.
- `people.to_df()` gives one column of the table per value, e.g. `immunity.sus_wild` and `immunity.sus_mutant` (or `_0`, `_1`, and so on for unnamed columns).

[Strains](building_diseases.qmd) use states like this to keep each person's immunity to each strain.

## Looking at people

`sim.people.to_df()` gives a table with a row for each agent and a column for each state (a state with several columns gives a column for each, e.g. `immunity.sus_wild`):

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=1000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
df = sim.people.to_df()
df.head()
```

This makes it easy to summarize people in your own way, e.g. the mean age of women and of men:

```{python}
df.groupby('female').age.mean()
```

`sim.people.person(10)` gives everything about one agent, here the one with UID 10:

```{python}
sim.people.person(10)
```

`sim.people.plot()` draws a histogram of each state of the people (`key=` for some of them), and `sim.people.plot_ages()` the age pyramid, as above.

### Deaths by cause

Each agent who dies has one cause, the module whose death it was: its name is in `people.causes`, and its position in that list in `people.cause_of_death`. Here measles kills about 1.6% of the people it infects (a death rate of 0.002 a day over 8 days infectious), alongside deaths from other causes:

```{python}
measles_deaths = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), ss.death(I, rate=ss.perday(0.002)), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate=ss.peryear(10), name='other') # Deaths from other causes, 10 per 1,000 people a year
sim = ss.Sim(measles_deaths, demographics=deaths, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()

ppl = sim.people
codes = ppl.cause_of_death[ppl.dead.uids] # The cause of each death
for code, cause in enumerate(ppl.causes):
    print('Deaths from', cause, '-', (codes == code).sum())
```

If two modules would kill the same person in the same step, one of them is chosen as the cause (see `request_death()` in [People](../api/people.qmd)), so no death is counted twice. In a module written as code, `people.died_of(module)` gives the agents who died of that module in the step just finished, e.g. to count deaths in a result of its own.

## In a compartmental run

In a compartmental run there are no agents. `sim.people` then has one row for each group the model is split into, and asking for a property of each person, such as `sim.people.age` in a model not split by age, raises an error saying to stratify by it or to run as agents. Results, `describe()`, and conditions such as `where=ss.person.age < 5` (for a model stratified by age) work the same either way.

The API reference for this page: [People](../api/people.qmd), [Arrays](../api/internals.arrays.qmd).

## Further reading

- [Mesa: AgentSet](https://mesa.readthedocs.io/latest/apis/agent.html): agents as Python objects, the alternative to keeping agents in arrays
- [LASER: Getting started](https://laser.idmod.org/laser-generic/): another framework that keeps agents' properties in arrays, one per property
- [NumPy: Indexing on ndarrays](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.indexing.html): the indexing that Starsim's arrays build on

## Appendix: looking at people

The properties and methods of `sim.people` for looking at the agents (see [People](../api/people.qmd) for all of them):

| Name | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `len(people)`, `people.n_alive` | The number of agents taking part, and the number of people they stand for |
| `people.auids` | The UIDs of the agents taking part (alive and not removed) |
| `people.alive`, `people.dead`, `people.female`, `people.male` | Who is alive, has died, is female, or is male, as states (`.uids` for their UIDs) |
| `people.age` | Each agent's age, in years |
| `people.parent` | The UID of each agent's mother, for agents born in the run (-1 for none) |
| `people.causes`, `people.cause_of_death` | The causes of death by name, and the cause of each agent's death (see [above](#deaths-by-cause)) |
| `people.died_of(module)` | The agents who died of a module in the step just finished, for code in a module |
| `people.keys()` | The names of the states of the people |
| `people.to_df()` | A table with a row for each agent and a column for each state |
| `people.person(uid)` | Everything about one agent |
| `people.brief()` | A one-line summary |
| `people.plot()` | A histogram of each state |
| `people.plot_ages()` | The age pyramid (`absolute=True` for numbers rather than shares) |

## Appendix: the kinds of array

The kinds of array that hold what agents are and have (see [Arrays](../api/internals.arrays.qmd)), for the states of `ss.People(extra_states=...)` and of modules:

| Array | Holds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `ss.BoolState` | True or false, for a state people are in that is worth counting (such as `alive`, `female`, or a disease's `I`): a module records the number in each of its states as a result | False |
| `ss.BoolArr` | True or false, for a flag used inside a module (such as `preterm`), with no result of its own; otherwise the same, with `.uids` for the agents for whom it is true | False |
| `ss.FloatArr` | A number, such as an age or a relative risk | NaN |
| `ss.IntArr` | A whole number, such as a count | -999999 (for none, since whole numbers have no NaN) |
| `ss.TimeArr` | The step on which something happened (such as `ti_dead`) | NaN |
| `ss.arrays.IndexArr` | The UID of another agent (such as `parent`), made by Starsim rather than by models | -1 |
| `ss.uids` | A set of UIDs, as from `(people.age < 5).uids`, for indexing any array | |

Each takes `default=`, a value or a distribution to draw each agent's value from, and `label=`, the name used in plots.
